the sensor responses of metallophthaloocyanine (Co, Ni, Cu) chemiresistors are exponentially related to analyte binding enthalpy and that the relative sensitivities of all metallophthalocyaines can be compared through a statistical analysis of their response patterns.
the sensitivities and response times of MPc chemiresistors are exponentially related to binding enthalpy and that MPc arrays can be used to identify analytes through pattern recognition techniques.

the sensitivities of metal-free and metallophthalocyaines to electron donors can be quantified by a simple exponential function, and that the relative sensitivities of the MPc chemiresistors are differentiable via statistical analysis.

the use of metallophthalo-cyanines for gas sensing.
the development of a sensor array for the detection and classification of a variety of analytes.
the design and fabrication of chemiresistor sensors based on phthalocyanines.

MPc sensors are capable of distinguishing among a wide range of analytes with high accuracy.
sensor responses correlate with binding enthalpies and that the binding enthalpies can be used to distinguish among the analytes, regardless their concentration.

The main takeaway from our work is that
MPc sensors can be used for the detection of a variety of electron donors and that the response magnitude and response time are predictable from binding thermodynamics.
MPc sensors are sensitive to a broad range of electron donor analytes and that their response magnitudes and recovery times depend strongly on the analyte binding enthalpy.
MPcs with similar electronic structures can exhibit similar response patterns to a given class of analyte, and thus, the use of an array of different MPcs is not necessary.
